note: Anything described as planned is not built. There is no demo behind these items, and this page will say so until there is.

built.name: Stable entity identifiers
built.detail: Every organisation and person carries a UID derived from a hash of its normalised name, with legal suffixes stripped. "OpenAI, Inc." and "OpenAI Global, LLC" resolve to one node. 308 entities are registered: 261 companies and 47 people, each with its alias set recorded so a new spelling joins the existing node instead of creating a second one.

built.name: A four-level taxonomy, not a menu
built.detail: 174 nodes: 1 root, 5 categories, 27 domains, and 141 sections. Navigation is generated from this tree, so a page's place in the structure is data rather than a hand-maintained menu, and a section that has no content yet is explicitly marked planned rather than quietly linked.

built.name: Cross-referencing that already resolves
built.detail: 108 entities currently appear in more than one place in the graph, which is the whole point: the company you meet as a defendant in a case is the same node you meet as the publisher of a tool and of an MCP server. Those pages link to each other because they share an identifier, not because someone remembered to link them.

built.name: A machine-readable surface
built.detail: Eleven JSON endpoints publish the underlying records, and llms.txt describes the site structure for retrieval systems. Every page carries a visible date stamp and a ready-made citation, so a model or a person quoting it can say when it was verified.

built.name: A registry of every published URL
built.detail: A daily stage reads the sitemap the site actually serves and records every live URL with the date it was first seen. It is how we know what exists, and a page that stops publishing is flagged rather than forgotten, because a URL that vanishes after being indexed needs a redirect.

built.name: Typed relationships between nodes
built.detail: Built. The graph carries 3,099 relationships across eleven named edge types, and every type states the method that produced it rather than asserting the link. A model cites a paper because the model authors put the arXiv id in their own Hub tags; a company is named in a lawsuit because the case record names it. The edges are published at the Relationships section and at /api/graph-relationships.json.

title: The Universal Knowledge Graph
answer:
This site is built as an entity graph rather than a pile of pages. Every organisation and person is a node with one stable identifier, so the same company is the same record whether it appears in the lawsuit tracker, the tools directory, or the MCP registry, however a source spelled its name. Today that graph holds 308 entities and 174 taxonomy nodes behind 3,107 published pages. The parts that are built are described below as built. The parts that are not are listed as planned, with no demo behind them.

This page is a section within Research, Knowledge and Learning, not a category of its own, because its subject is the wiring underneath the site rather than a body of content to browse. It exists as its own node for the same reason a company keeps one identifier no matter how many pages mention it: without a page that states the rule, a reader has no way to know that the OpenAI named on a lawsuit page and the OpenAI named on a tools page are the same organisation rather than a coincidence of naming.

The graph is what makes every other category on the site cross-reference the others instead of standing alone. A person profile in Ecosystem Entities, Market and Operations carries a stable identifier that the same profile reuses in AI Movers and Shakers and in any lawsuit or company page that names them. A model in Foundation Models, part of Technology and Core Infrastructure, links to the paper that introduced its architecture in the AI Research Library and to the company that released it in AI Companies. A state bill in AI Laws by State, under Enterprise Applications, Governance and Tools, links to the company or industry it would regulate. None of that cross-linking is manual. It exists because 3,099 typed relationships across eleven edge types connect these nodes, and each relationship states the method that produced it, a model cites a paper because the model's own Hub tags name it, a company appears in a lawsuit because the case record names it, rather than asserting a link with nothing behind it.

The Concept Taxonomy page, its sibling section here, does something narrower. It re-reads one particular chain of ideas rather than the whole graph. Together the two pages are the only ones on the site whose subject is its own structure rather than a fact about AI.

planned.name: Query by relationship
planned.detail: Asking for every compliance framework that applies to a given class of system, rather than searching for words that happen to appear near each other, needs typed edges first.

planned.name: Visual graph explorer
planned.detail: An interactive map of the graph is worth building once the edges carry meaning. Built earlier it would be a diagram of a filing system.

reading.body:
The site structures data as a graph of 308 stable entities (261 companies and 47 people) rather than separate pages, so the same organisation appears as one node whether it shows up in lawsuits, tool directories, or as a publisher.

This matters because AI research and deployment involve the same players across many roles. OpenAI is simultaneously a defendant, a tool publisher, and an MCP server operator. A unified record prevents the same entity from fragmenting into multiple nodes when different sources spell its name differently or use legal suffixes inconsistently. Today 108 entities appear in more than one place in the graph, with 3,099 typed relationships between them that cite their source rather than asserting them.

The graph is machine-readable at eleven JSON endpoints and tracks every published URL with the date it first appeared, so models and humans quoting this site can verify when information was current. A vanished page is flagged rather than forgotten. Planned features—querying by relationship type and a visual explorer—depend on the typed edges being complete first. The pages you read are navigation generated from the underlying taxonomy, not hand-maintained menus, which means a section marked planned has no demo behind it yet.

The data does not cover the timeline of how entities relate to compute, power, or buildings. That remains work for the individual pages the graph connects.

The graph solves a specific problem in coverage: any entity that moves between roles leaves traces in different parts of the site, and those traces need to point to the same record so readers encounter the full picture without manually cross-referencing. The cost of fragmentation is high because the players in AI are small and repeat. OpenAI appears in the lawsuit tracker, the tools registry, and the MCP server directory. Without stable identifiers, a reader looking at compliance liabilities would miss the tools the same entity publishes, and a researcher tracking compute dependencies would miss the legal constraints on the same operator. The graph prevents this by anchoring each organisation and person to a single UID derived from normalised names with legal suffixes stripped, so "OpenAI, Inc." and "OpenAI Global, LLC" resolve to one node.

The 3,099 relationships are typed, meaning each link carries a statement of its source rather than an assertion. When a model appears in a paper because the model authors put the arXiv ID in their own Hub tags, the edge records that method. When a company is named in a lawsuit, the edge records the case record as its source. This matters because it lets readers and systems distinguish between relationships that come from primary sources, secondary analysis, and inference. A reader can then decide whether to follow a connection or verify it against the original.

The infrastructure for citation and persistence is explicit. Every page carries a visible date stamp and ready-made citation so anything quoted from the site can be timestamped. The URL registry, built by reading the actual sitemap daily, records when each page first appeared and flags pages that stop publishing. This turns forgetting into a data problem instead of an operational accident.

What is a knowledge graph in this context?

A knowledge graph is a network of entities (organisations and people) connected by typed relationships that cite their sources. Each entity has one stable identifier, so the same organisation appears as a single record whether it is mentioned in lawsuits, tools directories, MCP registries, or other sections of the site.

How many entities are currently in the graph?

The graph holds 308 entities: 261 companies and 47 people. Each carries its alias set recorded, so a new spelling of the same entity joins the existing node instead of creating a second one.

Why does it matter that 108 entities appear in more than one place?

Those entities play multiple roles in AI research and deployment. When the same company appears as a defendant, a tool publisher, and an MCP server operator, a unified record prevents readers from treating them as separate entities and missing the connections between those roles.

How are the relationships documented?

The graph carries 3,099 relationships across eleven named edge types. Each relationship states the method that produced it: a model appears in a paper because the model authors cited it, a company is named in a lawsuit because the case record names it. The relationships are published at the Relationships section and at /api/graph-relationships.json.

Can I query the graph by asking which entities match a specific relationship type?

That feature is planned but not yet built. The underlying relationships are typed and sourced, but querying by relationship type rather than searching for words that happen to appear near each other requires that work to be completed first.

How can I verify when information on the site was current?

Every page carries a visible date stamp and a ready-made citation format. The site also maintains a daily registry of every live URL with the date it was first seen, so you can check when a page was first published and whether it is still active.
